hypothesis.hypothesis:
Insert a 4-entry circular instruction queue between the PC/predictor
and ID. The front end runs ahead of the back end by up to four
instructions; the predictor still predicts at fetch time.

Entry payload (flops, no reset needed): pc[31:2], instr[31:0],
pred_taken, bht_ctr[1:0], alt_target[31:2] (~97 bits). Control flops
(reset / flushed): wptr_q[1:0], rptr_q[1:0], count_q[2:0] plus
registered empty_q = (count==0) and full_q = (count==4) flags so no
consumer decodes the count combinationally.

Fetch side (if_stage):
  fetch_ok = imem_ready && !full_q            // flops only
  PC:  redirect ? redirect_target
     : fetch_ok ? (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4)
     : pc
  The PC enable no longer reads load_use (imem word -> rs compare),
  dmem_stall or div_stall: the imem -> load-use -> stall_if -> PC path
  disappears. The fetched word + prediction are written into
  buf[wptr_q] whenever fetch_ok, UNCONDITIONALLY (not gated by
  redirect or by ID's stall): the ~390 payload flops' write enable is
  then a function of two flops (imem_ready LFSR, full_q) and a 2-bit
  pointer decode, keeping stall_id / redirect fanout exactly where it
  is today. Whether that write is "real" is decided purely by the
  pointer/count update.

Decode side:
  head      = empty_q ? {pc, imem_data, pred_taken, bht_ctr, alt_target}   // live bypass
                      : buf[rptr_q]
  head_valid = !empty_q || imem_ready
  Both selects are registered (empty_q, rptr_q), so ID sees one
  flop-selected mux level (4:1 + bypass) in front of the decoder,
  imm_gen, regfile read addresses, ID forward compares and the
  load-use compare. In the FPGA bench imem_data is an LFSR flop, so
  this path starts at a flop and is far from the 10.26 ns EX cone.
  The IF/ID bundle handed to id_stage is {head.pc, head.instr,
  head_valid, head.pred_taken, head.bht_ctr, head.alt_target}; ID is
  otherwise unchanged (ID/EX control flops ANDed with valid as today).

Pointer update (small control flops only):
  enq = fetch_ok;  deq = head_valid && !stall_id
  redirect -> wptr = rptr = 0, count = 0 (queue flushed; the fetch
              this cycle is on the wrong path and discarded; PC loads
              the target as today)
  else      -> wptr += enq; rptr += deq; count += enq - deq
  The empty-bypass case (count 0, fetch_ok, deq) writes the word into
  buf[wptr] AND advances both pointers, so it is net-empty and needs
  no special data path. count never underflows because deq with
  empty_q requires imem_ready, which implies enq (full_q is 0).

Hazard unit: stall_if is no longer used for the PC (keep or delete
the output); flush_if becomes !head_valid; stall_id / flush_id /
stall_ex_mem / hold_mem_wb are unchanged, with load-use now
comparing id_ex_rd against head.instr[19:15]/[24:20]. Redirect keeps
priority over everything and remains a control-only flush of ID/EX
and the queue pointers (no payload clear, per the r3s0 lesson about
192-fanout reset nets).

Retirement order, RVFI, the EX/MEM/WB pipeline, BHT training and the
mispredict-only redirect are unchanged, so formal and cosim contracts
hold by construction; pc_rdata of each retirement is still the
queued pc and pc_wdata chain is untouched.

Expected: cycles 4.19M -> ~3.96-4.0M (-4.5% to -6%), Fmax neutral to
slightly positive (load-use/dmem_stall/div_stall removed from the PC
enable; r4s1 showed the same queue shape was Fmax-neutral on r3s0).
Net fitness about +5% to +6%.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r5s1 (regression, -11.41%): Porting r4s1's fetch queue onto the r4s2 predictor core as a 4-entry pointer queue scored 206.22 against 232.78, so Fmax must have fallen at least ~11% (to ~86 MHz if cycles stayed at 4,188,685, or ~82 MHz if they reached the ~4.0M estimate; inferred, since no cycles or timing report were recorded), and the likely cause is the combinational ID head mux (empty_q ? live imem word : buf[rptr_q], eight inputs per bit): on r3s0, r4s1's 2-entry head mux merged with the existing imem_ready NOP mux into one LUT4 per bit, which is why it was Fmax-neutral, but r4s2 had deleted that NOP mux and fed the raw imem word to ID, so here the head mux adds about two new LUT levels at the start of the imem word -> decoder/use_imm -> opb pre-select -> regfile read -> ID/EX cone, which r5s0's timing report put only 0.17 ns off the worst path (P4), even though the hypothesis called it slack-rich because it "starts at a flop"; so a front-end change is Fmax-free only if it replaces a mux already on the instruction word, and before adding a queue, re-time that cone and prefer a registered queue head (ID decodes from a flop, at the cost of one extra cycle per EX redirect) over a wide combinational head select.

title: Speculate predicted branches past the load-use hazard: a branch that consumes the LOAD in EX issues without the bubble and is resolved one stage later (MEM) against MEM/WB.wb_data, with a registered late redirect
motivation:
Trace study of the timed CoreMark region (ISS, 2,922,015 retired insns,
champion = 4,188,685 cycles, CPI 1.43):
  - Classic predictor headroom is almost gone. The 512x2b bimodal BHT
    mispredicts 39,772 of 529,588 branches; gshare/tournament (up to 2K
    entries) only reach 32.6k-36k. All 13,735 JALRs are returns and an
    8-entry RAS would hit 13,734. Mispredicts plus returns total ~53.5k
    cycles (1.3%), and a better direction predictor recovers ~0.2%.
  - Load-use is the largest remaining non-istall stall: 203,959 adjacent
    LOAD->consumer pairs, and 135,320 (66%) have a conditional BRANCH as
    the consumer (list walks, `if (*p == x)`, state machine loops). The
    next largest classes are load->load-address (59k) and load->ALU (9k).
    Under the 22% istall model roughly 0.78 of these pairs arrive back
    to back, so load->branch costs ~105k cycles, about 2.5% of the run,
    which is twice all remaining mispredicts and returns combined.
The branch was already predicted in IF and the right path is already
being fetched, so the load-use bubble in front of it buys nothing unless
the prediction is wrong. That is a predictor problem: speculate on the
prediction instead of stalling.
Timing (make timing, place_option 0, 91.55 MHz): the ALU/DSP cone
(opa_val/fwda_wb -> alu_result, 16.22 ns) is tied with the EX redirect
cone (MEM/WB.wb_data -> fwd mux -> 32b compare -> redirect -> pc_q,
16.19 ns, 33 cells). Any new logic must stay off both.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Late-resolve load-dependent branches.
1. Hazard. When the ID-stage word is an aligned-target BRANCH (use
   if_stage's existing is_br && !imm1 predecode, exported in if_id_t) and
   the load-use compare fires against the LOAD in ID/EX, do not stall.
   The branch enters ID/EX with late=1 and its six one-hot sel_* are
   routed into late_sel_* flops (EX's sel_* are zero for it, so the EX
   redirect equation and its path are unchanged). late1/late2 record
   which operand matched the load (these are the registered fwd1_ex /
   fwd2_ex matches). Misaligned-target branches, JALR, and every
   non-branch consumer keep today's load-use stall.
2. EX. A late branch only passes its prediction, its sel bits,
   alt_target, bht_ctr and the post-forward rs1/rs2 (already in EX/MEM
   for RVFI) into EX/MEM. It does no EX redirect and no EX BHT training.
3. MEM. The load is now in MEM/WB, so its wb_data is a flop. Build the
   operands as op1 = late1 ? MEM/WB.wb_data : EX/MEM.rs1_val (and op2 the
   same way; flop-driven selects), then take eq/lt/ltu and AND-OR them
   with late_sel_* to get late_mis. Register late_mis and alt_target into
   late_redirect_q / late_target_q (all flop-to-flop, a short cone). The
   same cycle, write the BHT training for late branches from MEM.
4. Late redirect (the next cycle, while the branch sits in WB). The
   registered late_redirect_q loads pc_q with late_target_q. It is only
   an early-arriving flop side input on the PC mux, so the co-critical
   EX redirect path gets no new compare depth; any EX redirect that
   cycle is ignored. It also flushes ID/EX (control-only, as now), kills
   the EX/MEM capture (valid, reg_write, mem_read, mem_write,
   is_illegal, is_branch, late, and no BHT write), and aborts or blocks
   a div_unit start from the wrong-path instruction in EX (add an
   abort-to-IDLE input). Only the two instructions behind the branch
   are wrong-path, and neither has written memory or the regfile: a
   store in EX writes only in MEM, and it is killed at capture.
5. RVFI. In MEM, rs?_val is corrected with the MEM/WB value and pc_next
   is recomputed (branch_target vs pc+4) from the late outcome before
   MEM/WB, so RVFI rs1/rs2_rdata and pc_wdata stay exact (RVFI-only,
   pruned in the timed netlist).
Cost/benefit: every back-to-back load->branch saves its bubble (~105k
cycles). A mispredicted late branch costs 3 cycles instead of today's
stall+1 = 2 (~+8-10k cycles at a ~7.5% mispredict rate), which is
~95k cycles net, about -2.3% cycles. Fmax should hold because the new
compare runs flop->flop in MEM and reaches the PC only through a
registered select, and the load-use hazard gains only a single AND term
(is_br_ok) that arrives as early as the existing rs compare.

title: Stack r5s0's registered-select Fmax cuts with r5s2's load->branch late resolve on the r4s2 champion
motivation:
Round 5 produced two measured, orthogonal gains on the r4s2 champion
(232.78 = 10 x 97.505 MHz / 4,188,685 cycles). Neither cleared the 4.6%
bar alone:
  * r5s0 (241.93, +3.93%) is pure timing: registered, priority-resolved
    one-hot forward selects, sign-gated DSP extension bits, a one-hot
    group-select ALU, a single 33-bit borrow compare with a 2-level
    redirect, and opcode-bit use_imm/use_pc. Its seeds were
    [100.146, 101.336, 101.336] MHz with cycles unchanged, and its
    worst path became MEM/WB.wb_data -> fwd -> ALU -> alu_result
    (6 cells).
  * r5s2 (239.29, +2.80%) is pure IPC. A predicted aligned BRANCH that
    consumes the LOAD in ID/EX skips the load-use bubble and resolves
    one cycle later in MEM, with a registered late redirect. Cycles
    fell from 4,188,685 to 4,056,705 (-3.15%), and the median Fmax held
    at 97.07. Its seed-0 placement dropped to 84.2 MHz on the old
    33-cell wb_data -> fwd mux -> compare -> redirect -> pc_q cone
    (17.17 ns, 11 cells), which is the cone r5s0 flattens.
LESSONS says to stack the two instead of re-proposing either alone. If
they compound: 10 x 101.3e6 / 4,056,705 = 249.8, or +7.3%, which clears
the bar with margin.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Implement both changes together on the current r4s2 RTL. Most of the
work is r5s0's select-registering, the micro_opt part.
A. Registered, qualified forward selects (r4s0/r5s0). ex_stage exports
   ex_rw_next = ID/EX.reg_write && !misalign_jump (JALR uses a 2-bit
   carry for agu_sum[1]). mem_stage exports
   wb_rw_next = EX/MEM.reg_write && !mem_misalign. ID computes one-hot
   sel_ex = ex_rw_next && match_ex and
   sel_wb = wb_rw_next && match_wb && !sel_ex per consumer (rs1, rs2,
   alu_a, alu_b; alu_a/alu_b masked by use_pc/use_imm). It registers
   them, duplicated per 16-bit half, and zeroes the rs?_val/opa/opb
   payload flop when a forward is selected. Each EX operand is then one
   flop-driven AND-OR, (ex & sel_ex) | (wb & sel_wb) | val_q, and EX
   stops reading the fanout-130 live reg_write flops.
B. DSP 33rd operand bits come from their own sign-gated registered
   selects, in parallel with bit 31 and not in series after it.
C. ALU: a flop-selected one-hot group AND-OR (add/sub adder whose
   33-bit borrow gives SLT/SLTU, logic unit, shifter, LUI) instead of
   the 5-bit case mux. The DSP output meets one final LUT
   (mul_lo/mul_hi/nonmul). Keep the post-DSP OR tree under
   (* syn_keep = 1 *) so synthesis cannot re-associate OR levels after
   the DSP output (a LESSONS note).
D. Branch compare: one 33-bit borrow compare with a registered
   cmp_unsigned bit, and 4 prediction-folded one-hot selects
   (eq/ne/lt/ge). The redirect is the 2-level form
   (s_eq&eq)|(s_ne&!eq)|(s_lt&lt)|(s_ge&!lt)|(is_jalr&!agu1).
E. use_imm/use_pc/is_jump_f are LUT3s of opcode bits, taken off the
   decoder cone that feeds the opb pre-select.
F. r5s2 late load->branch resolve. When the ID word is an aligned
   BRANCH (if_stage's is_br && !imm1, exported in if_id_t) and the
   load-use compare hits, do not stall. The branch enters ID/EX with
   late=1 and its compare selects go into separate late_sel_* flops, so
   EX's sel_* are 0 and neither the EX redirect equation nor BHT
   training fires in EX. late1/late2 record which operand matched the
   load. The timeline, with load L and late branch B:
     t1: L in MEM, B in EX, B+1 in ID. B does nothing in EX (no
         redirect, no BHT training). EX/MEM captures its post-forward
         rs?_val as usual.
     t2: L in WB, B in MEM. Operand = late? ? MEM/WB.wb_data :
         EX/MEM.rs?_val (flop-selected). The eq/borrow compare AND-ORs
         with late_sel_* into late_mis, which is registered as
         late_redirect_q with late_target_q = alt_target. This is a
         flop-to-flop cone that never touches the PC combinationally.
         EX/MEM holds B, which is not a memory op, so no dmem stall is
         possible this cycle.
     t3: late_redirect_q=1 (a 1-cycle pulse). pc_q <- late_target_q at
         the highest priority after reset, above the EX redirect,
         because B is older than anything in EX. It kills three
         younger instructions:
         - B+1 in MEM: gate dmem_wen/dmem_ren with !late_redirect_q.
           Mask the dmem_stall term (ex_mem_mem_op && !late_redirect_q)
           so the kill cannot be frozen. MEM/WB captures valid=0,
           reg_write=0.
         - B+2 in EX: EX/MEM captures a bubble. No BHT training.
           div_unit aborts to IDLE.
         - B+3 in ID: ID/EX control-only flush.
   All kill inputs are early-arriving flop side inputs. The late
   mispredict penalty is 3 cycles, against 1 (load-use) + 2 today. BHT
   training for B is registered from MEM at t2. If it collides with an
   EX-trainer write in the same cycle, the older (MEM) write wins; the

title: Two-stage front end: 128-entry L0 instruction loop cache that supplies the fetch when imem is not ready, plus a registered IF/ID stage so the cache read never lands on the decode cone
motivation:
The champion (r4s2: 232.78, 97.5 MHz, 4,188,685 cycles for 2,922,015
retired instructions, CPI 1.43) is fetch-bandwidth bound. imem_ready is
an independent xorshift draw every cycle (fpga/bench_stall_gen.sv and
test/cosim/main.cpp bus_accepts_main(): ~22% not-ready whether or not a
fetch is wanted), so the front end delivers at most 0.78 instr/cycle.
About 0.28 istall cycles are paid per fetched instruction, roughly
800k of the 1.27M non-retiring cycles. Everything else is small:
load-use ~160k, dstall ~250k, mispredicts + JALR ~54k (per r5s2's trace
study).
Every earlier attack on istall only reshuffled fetch slots: r4s1/r5s1's
fetch queues bank a word only when the back end happens to stall.
r5s1's 4-entry queue got 3,957,016 cycles (-5.5%) but lost 16% Fmax to
its combinational head mux in front of the decoder. None of them can
beat the 0.78 cap. CoreMark spends the timed window in a few small hot
loops: core_state_transition, matrix_mul_*, crcu8/16, core_list_find,
mergesort + cmp_*. An on-core copy of those words removes the cap. When
imem is not ready the word can come from the core instead of the bus.
ARCHITECTURE.md allows logic that hides stalls, and CLAUDE.md allows
caches, but no hypothesis has tried a cache yet (grep log.jsonl).
The r5s1 lesson gives the timing rule: a front-end change is Fmax-free
only if ID decodes from a flop. So the cache has to sit in front of a
registered IF/ID stage. That costs one extra cycle per EX redirect
(~54k cycles, 1.3%), which is small next to the istall cycles it hides.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split fetch into F (PC + L0 lookup + predictor) and a registered IF/ID
stage, and add a direct-mapped L0 instruction cache in F.

1. L0 cache (new rtl/l0_icache.sv, instantiated in if_stage).
   * 128 entries, direct-mapped, index = pc_q[8:2]. Async-read
     distributed RAM (* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *), read
     address = pc_q, the same flop that already indexes the BHT, so
     the read runs in parallel with the fetch. Do NOT use BSRAM. Its
     synchronous read would need pc_d (next PC) as the address, which
     puts the BSRAM on the co-critical redirect -> pc_q cone.
   * Data per entry (64 bits): instr[31:0]; tgt[31:2], the predicted
     target pc+imm computed by the existing carry-select adder at fill
     time (static for a given pc and word, so a hit needs no adder);
     and two predecode bits, jal_ok = is_jal && !imm1 and
     br_ok = is_br && !imm1.
   * Tag: pc[19:9] in the same LUTRAM (or a parallel one). Valid bits:
     128 flops with synchronous reset, read by a 128:1 mux on pc_q[8:2]
     (in parallel with the LUTRAM read). Hit also requires
     pc_q[31:20] == 0, computed from the PC flop in parallel.
     Out-of-range PCs never hit.
   * Fill: every cycle imem_ready = 1, write
     {imem_data, pred_target_imem, jal_ok, br_ok, tag} at pc_q[8:2] and
     set valid. This does not depend on stalls or redirect: the word at
     pc_q is architecturally correct whenever the bus accepts. The
     write address and WE come from flops, and the data from the
     existing IF adder, which is short.
   * Coherence: FENCE / FENCE.I (opcode 0001111, already decoded as a
     NOP) flash-clears all 128 valid flops when it is valid in EX. The
     RISC-V spec needs no more than that. If any bench program
     (selftest/random*.S) stores into its own code without FENCE.I,
     also clear valid[mem_addr[8:2]] on a store in MEM (the 128 valid
     flops make this a cheap second write port).
2. F stage (if_stage.sv). Word source select = imem_ready, a flop:
     word    = imem_ready ? imem_data            : l0.instr
     pt      = imem_ready ? pred_taken_imem      : (l0.jal_ok | (l0.br_ok & bht_ctr[1]))
     ptgt    = imem_ready ? pred_target_imem     : l0.tgt
     fetch_ok = imem_ready | l0_hit
   The imem-side predictor path is unchanged apart from one final
   flop-selected mux. The L0 side is pc_q -> LUTRAM -> mux -> PC D,
   with no adder. PC update:
     redirect ? redirect_target
     : (fetch_ok && ifid_can_accept) ? (pt ? ptgt : pc+4)
     : hold
   redirect stays the last mux level on pc_q, so the EX redirect cone
   (P2 in r5s0's report) gets no new depth. ifid_can_accept is built
   from flops only (see 3).
3. IF/ID register (new flops, in if_stage or a small if_id register
   block). Payload: pc, instr, pred_taken, bht_ctr, alt_target, valid.
   * Capture when !ifid_valid_q || !stall_id_backend, where
     stall_id_backend = load_use | dmem_stall | div_stall. This lets an
     empty IF/ID fill while the back end is frozen, which gives one
     entry of decoupling for free.
   * valid_d = fetch_ok. On redirect, valid is cleared (control-only,
     one flop, per LESSONS r3s0) and the PC loads the target.
   * ID (id_stage.sv) reads if_id_q instead of the combinational
     bundle. Its decoder, imm_gen, regfile addresses, forward compares
     and the load-use compare in hazard_unit all start from flops, just
     as they start from the LFSR flop in today's timed netlist. P4
     (imem word -> decoder -> use_imm -> opb -> ID/EX) keeps its length
     and does not see the L0 read.
   * hazard_unit: flush_if / imem_stall no longer drive ID (ID's
     bubble comes from !if_id_q.valid). stall_if is replaced by the
     IF/ID accept logic above. load_use now compares if_id_q rs fields
     (flops) against ID/EX.rd.
   * Mispredict / JALR penalty grows from 2 to 3 cycles (+~54k cycles).
     Predicted-taken BRANCH/JAL still redirect in F with no bubble,
     because the prediction is made on the F word, as today.
4. RVFI, EX, MEM, WB and the divider are unchanged. nret stays 1.

Measured hit rate: I ran an ISS trace (test/cosim/reference.py on a
-O3 TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000 CoreMark build, start/stop markers, 2,922,015
fetches, the same count as r5s2) through a direct-mapped
fill-on-every-fetch model. The per-fetch hit rate is 71.5% at 64
entries, 83.3% at 128 and 93.8% at 256, stable across the whole run.
Expected cycles: about h * ~800k istall cycles are hidden, minus ~54k
for the longer redirect. At h = 0.83 (128 entries) that is ~3.58M
cycles (-14.5%). At h = 0.94 (256 entries) it is ~3.49M (-17%). Area: ~128 x 76 bits of LUTRAM plus 128 valid
flops and the muxes, roughly +900-1200 LUT4 (3.6k -> ~4.8k, well under
the 10k target). Fmax risk: the new cones start at pc_q and imem_ready
flops and end at pc_q / IF/ID flops. They are about as deep as today's
pc_q -> BHT LUTRAM -> pred_taken -> PC path, so budget 0-4% Fmax loss.
Net ~+10%.

If the implementer's timing run shows the L0 read cone is critical,
drop to 64 entries (index pc_q[7:2]) before dropping anything else.
If there is slack and LUT headroom, 256 entries (pc_q[9:2]) raises the
hit rate further.

title: EX-free control flow: verify every branch/JALR in MEM (load->branch bubble gone) plus an 8-entry IF return-address stack
motivation:
Trace data already in log.jsonl (ISS, timed CoreMark window, 2,922,015
insns; champion r4s2 = 4,188,685 cycles, CPI 1.43):
  - Direction-prediction headroom is nearly exhausted: the 512x2b bimodal
    BHT mispredicts 39,772 of 529,588 branches and gshare/tournament up
    to 2K entries only reach 32.6k-36k.
  - All 13,735 JALRs are returns and an 8-entry RAS would hit 13,734; today
    each one redirects from EX (2 bubbles, ~27.5k cycles, 0.66%).
  - 135,320 of the 203,959 adjacent LOAD->consumer pairs have a
    conditional branch as the consumer. r5s2 removed that bubble for
    predicted aligned branches only and measured 4,056,705 cycles (-3.15%)
    with Fmax unchanged (97.07 MHz), but kept the EX redirect as well,
    so it added a second redirect source and its worst path became
    MEM/WB.wb_data -> EX forward -> compare -> redirect -> pc_q (17.17 ns).
The EX branch compare -> redirect -> pc_q/ID-EX-flush cone is one of the
tied cones at ~16.2 ns on the champion (the other is the
MEM/WB.wb_data -> forward -> ALU/DSP cone, the champion's worst path).
No direction-predictor change can pass the 4.6% bar alone. Taking control
flow out of EX entirely does two things at once: it removes the
load->branch bubble and returns from the cycle count, and it removes one
of the tied Fmax cones.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make EX redirect-free. Every control-flow check runs one stage later in
MEM from registered inputs. IF adds a RAS so that returns stop
mispredicting, which pays for the extra cycle a late mispredict costs.

1. Branch verification in MEM (all branches, uniform):
   - EX still forwards rs1/rs2 as today. It no longer computes redirect.
     Instead it registers the three comparator results (eq, lt, ltu) into
     EX/MEM (cmp_*_q). This cone ends at a flop with fanout 1, not at
     pc_q and the flush net. EX/MEM also carries the one-hot mispredict
     selects sel_* (unchanged ID logic, prediction already folded in),
     alt_target, pred, bht_ctr, and a late1/late2 flag per operand.
   - late? = ID/EX's fwd?_ex match && the producer now in EX/MEM is a LOAD
     (EX/MEM.ctrl.mem_to_reg). Only in that case is the EX-forwarded
     operand stale. Otherwise MEM redirects from flops only:
       redirect_mem = AND-OR(sel_*_q, cmp_*_q)   (2 LUT levels)
     For a late branch, MEM re-runs the compare with the stale operand
     replaced by MEM/WB.wb_data (the load is always in MEM/WB when the
     branch is in EX/MEM, because the two registers advance together and
     a branch is never a mem op, so dmem_stall can't split them). That
     cone is MEM/WB.wb_data -> flop-selected 2:1 -> compare -> redirect.
     It is one forward level shorter than today's EX cone.
   - hazard_unit: load_use_hazard is suppressed when the ID instruction is
     a BRANCH (opcode 1100011 from the raw word). A branch uses rs1/rs2
     only for the compare, so it can issue right behind its load.
     JALR, stores and ALU consumers keep the bubble.
2. JALR verification in MEM + RAS in IF:
   - IF predecodes JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5} as a push of pc+4, and a
     JALR with rd=x0 and rs1 in {x1,x5} as a pop. A pop is predicted
     taken to the top of stack (a flop) when its imm[1] is 0 and the RAS
     is non-empty. The top of stack adds one flop-sourced input to the
     prediction mux, ahead of the redirect mux.
   - The RAS is an 8x30-bit circular buffer with a 3-bit TOS pointer.
     Pushes and pops happen only on a valid, non-stalled IF cycle. Each
     instruction carries the post-op pointer (3 bits) down the pipe, and
     a MEM redirect restores it. Contents are not repaired: a rare
     corruption costs performance only.
   - The predicted JALR target travels in the existing alt_target field.
     In MEM: jalr_redirect = is_jalr && (!pred || EX/MEM.mem_addr[31:2] !=
     pred_target[31:2] || misaligned). mem_addr already holds
     agu_sum = rs1 + imm. Target = {mem_addr[31:2],2'b00}, or pc+4 when
     agu_sum[1] traps (this keeps the pc_fwd contract). Unpredicted JALRs
     (none in the timed window) cost 3 bubbles instead of 2.
3. Redirect plumbing from MEM:
   - The PC D-mux keeps redirect as its last level. Its target is
     late_tgt = is_jalr ? {mem_addr[31:2],00} : alt_target_q (all flops).
   - One redirect kills three wrong-path instructions: the IF word (PC
     load), ID/EX (control-only flush as today), and the instruction in
     EX. That last one gets its EX/MEM control bits cleared (valid,
     reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, is_branch, is_jalr, is_div,
     is_illegal, sel_*), so a wrong-path store or load never reaches the

title: Five-cone de-merge: kept 2-level redirect + 1-LUT flush, load-use off the ID/EX data enable, flat one-hot ALU, split L0/regfile index fanout
motivation:
`make timing TARGET=bench` on the r6s1 champion (87.4 MHz, 3,552,529
cycles, fitness 246.35) shows FIVE distinct cones within 0.03 ns of each
other (data delay ~11.40 ns, 200 MHz constraint, 2583 violating
endpoints). One cut alone therefore buys nothing (LESSONS r5s0/r6s0);
every cone has to shrink together. The cones, as read cell by cell from
generated/timing/gowin_p0/impl/pnr/core_bench.tr:
 C1 (paths 1,2,4,5,8,12-15,19,22-24) EX/MEM.alu_result_15 -> 2.1 ns route
    -> rs2 forward LUT -> 17-cell compare carry chain -> THREE LUTs named
    u_if/pc_en_s11 -> pc_en_s5 -> pc_en_s1 (synthesis spliced the redirect
    OR-tree into pc_en = redirect | fetch_ok&accept) -> TWO more LUTs
    u_id/n280_s2 -> n280_s0 (flush = (load_use|redirect)&!dmem_stall,
    OR reset) -> RESET pin of ID/EX valid_q / sel_*_q. Also pc_q D,
    idx_vld_q D and bht_wdata D. 5 LUT levels after the compare where 3
    are enough.
 C2 (paths 3,9,11,18) ID/EX.opa_val -> 2-LUT forward mux (alu_a_s1,s2)
    -> 2.4 ns route -> 27-cell adder chain -> 4-5 LUT levels of case(op)
    result mux (alu_result_26_s14,s13,s7,...) + div OR + MUL mux.
 C3 (paths 6,7,20,21,25) IF/ID.instr_17 (rs1 bit, fanout into the whole
    32x32 regfile read mux: 3.97 ns route) -> 4 LUTs (load-use compare
    -> stall, merged by synthesis with the rs1_addr==0 read case) ->
    RESET pin of ID/EX.rs1_val. The ID/EX datapath flops use a sync
    reset that folds !stall (incl. load_use) with x0-read, so the
    load-use compare sits in front of ~400 datapath flops.
 C4 (path 10) imem word (lfsr_7) -> imm_lo -> lo_sum carry chain -> FOUR
    LUTs tgt_hi_29_s10 -> tgt_hi_24_s10 -> tgt_hi_26_s8 -> s7 (the
    carry-select was meant to be one LUT5; synthesis re-derived the
    pc_hi +-1 carries inside it) -> ptgt mux -> pc_d (2) -> pc_q.
 C5 (paths 16,17) L0 index copy idx_dat_q_2 -> 3.72 ns route (one copy
    drives all 64 bits x 8 LUTRAM banks) -> LUTRAM -> 3-level bank mux
    -> pt (2 LUTs) -> pc_d (2) -> index copies.
Every one of these has at least one LUT level or one long route that is
a synthesis artefact of merged/shared logic or of one flop driving a
huge fanout, not an inherent dependency. None of the cuts changes the
cycle count (bit-identical IPC), so this is pure Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cut all five tied cones with local, IPC-neutral restructuring. Build ALL
groups before evaluating (a tied cone left uncut sets the period); run
`make timing TARGET=bench` after groups 1-3 and again at the end.

GROUP 1 - C1 redirect / flush tail (ex_stage, hazard_unit, id_stage, if_stage)
 a. In ex_stage declare `(* syn_keep = 1 *) logic redirect_k;` computed
    as the existing flat AND-OR of sel_* with cmp_eq/cmp_lt/cmp_ltu plus
    is_jalr&!agu_sum[1] (same equation), and drive `redirect` from it, so
    synthesis cannot re-associate it into the pc_en OR-tree (target: 2
    LUT levels after the compare chain, not 3).
 b. hazard_unit: compute from flops only, as kept nets:
      no_dstall   = !( !dmem_ready && ex_mem_mem_op )
      clr_early   = reset || (load_use_hazard && no_dstall)
    and export `id_clr = clr_early || (redirect && no_dstall)` so the
    ID/EX control-flop clear (currently `reset || flush`, 2 LUTs after
    redirect) is ONE LUT3 after redirect. id_stage uses `if (id_clr)`
    for the control flops (reset is inside id_clr). Pass reset into
    hazard_unit.
 c. if_stage: `(* syn_keep = 1 *)` on fa = fetch_ok && accept, and
    pc_en = redirect || fa, so the PC enable is one LUT after redirect.
GROUP 2 - C3 ID datapath enable / regfile read (hazard_unit, id_stage, reg_file, if_stage)
 a. The ID/EX datapath flops (data_q) only need to HOLD on dmem_stall or
    div_stall; on a load-use bubble the control flops are cleared, so
    the datapath is don't-care and may be overwritten (X stays in IF/ID
    and is re-captured next cycle). Export `hold_id_data = dmem_stall ||
    div_stall` (flop-sourced, 1 LUT) and use `if (!hold_id_data)` for
    data_q. load_use is exclusive with div_stall (a DIV is never a
    LOAD), so control-flop behaviour is unchanged.
 b. reg_file: drop the `rs?_addr == 0 -> 0` read arm. regs[0] is reset
    to 0 and never written, so the plain read already returns 0; the
    write-first bypass is qualified with a precomputed
    `w_en_nz = w_en && (w_addr != 0)` (MEM/WB flops only, NOP
    `addi x0` must not bypass). This stops Gowin from folding x0 and
    !stall into the rs?_val sync RESET.
 c. if_stage IF/ID register: add `(* syn_preserve = 1 *)` copies
    rf_rs1_q / rf_rs2_q of instr[19:15] / instr[24:20] (same enable as
    data_q.instr) that feed ONLY the regfile read address; the original
    instr bits keep feeding decode, hazard and forward compares. Route
    them to id_stage through if_id_t (new fields) and use them for
    rs1_addr/rs2_addr to the regfile.
GROUP 3 - C2 ALU (alu.sv, ex_stage; interface of `alu` unchanged so
test_alu.py keeps passing)
 a. Decode the flop-driven `op` inside the ALU into kept one-hot
    selects (s_as, s_cmp, s_logic + 2-bit logic code, s_sll, s_srx +
    arith, s_lui); they settle while the adder chain is still running.
 b. One 33-bit add/sub serves ADD/SUB/SLT/SLTU:
    sum33 = {ae,a} + ({be,b} ^ {33{sub}}) + sub, sub = SUB|SLT|SLTU,
    ae/be = operand sign for SLT, 0 otherwise; lt = sum33[32].
 c. nonmul[i] = (s_as & sum[i]) | logic[i] | (s_sll & sll[i]) |
    (s_srx & srx[i]) | (s_lui & b[i]) | div_in[i] | (i==0 & s_cmp & lt),
    written as a flat OR under `(* syn_keep = 1 *)`, then the single
    flop-selected MUL mux last (mul_sel ? (mul_hi ? p_hi : p_lo) :
    nonmul). ALTOPS MUL branch untouched.
 d. ex_stage forward muxes: precompute kept one-hot selects from flops,
    selX_ex = fwdX_ex & ex_mem_w_en, selX_wb = fwdX_wb & mem_wb_w_en &
    !selX_ex, selX_rf = !(selX_ex|selX_wb), for rs1/rs2/alu_a/alu_b, so
    each operand bit is one AND-OR (LUT5) instead of two LUT levels.
GROUP 4 - C4/C5 IF next-PC (if_stage, l0_icache)
 a. `(* syn_keep = 1 *)` on pc_hi_p1, pc_hi_m1 (computed from pc_q
    only) and on the lo_sum carry-out, so tgt_hi is ONE LUT5 select
    after the carry chain instead of the 4 levels in the report.
 b. Split l0_icache dat_mem into dat_i (instr[31:0], feeds only IF/ID)
    and dat_p (tgt[31:2], jal_ok, br_ok; feeds pt/ptgt -> pc_d), each
    with its own `(* syn_preserve = 1 *)` index copy (idx_dat_i,
    idx_dat_p, same D/enable as pc_q), halving the index fanout on the
    pc_d cone. Contents/behaviour unchanged.

Correctness: no architectural behaviour changes. Group 2a changes only
don't-care datapath of a bubble; 2b is equivalent because regs[0] is
constant 0 and the bypass keeps the x0 guard; group 3 is bit-exact per
op (test_alu.py vectors); all others are attributes / net splits.

title: Registered redirect with a fetch-override: EX writes mispredict/JALR into flops and F fetches the target from them the next cycle, so the redirect cone ends in one flop at no extra penalty
motivation:
The r6s1 champion (87.5 MHz, 3,552,529 cycles) is limited by the EX redirect
cone: its worst path runs EX/MEM.alu_result -> EX forward mux -> 32-bit compare
-> redirect AND-OR -> flush_id / pc_en -> ID/EX valid_q (10 logic levels, 24
cells, u_ex -> u_if -> u_id). r5s2's worst path was the same cone ending at
pc_q. The combinational redirect is the only EX signal that fans out into three
other stages (pc_q plus its three L0 index copies as mux select and clock
enable, IF/ID valid, the ID/EX control flops), so it pays both the compare
depth and a ~100-load tail. A plain registered redirect would add a cycle to
each of the ~100k mispredicts/JALRs (~+2.8% cycles). But the fetch side can
absorb that cycle: the bench's imem data is an LFSR flop and io_imemAddr only
feeds an XOR to the LEDs, so putting a flop-selected mux in front of the fetch
address costs almost nothing on the imem side.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split control-flow resolution across the EX/MEM boundary without lengthening
the mispredict penalty.
(1) EX keeps the same sel_* x comparator AND-OR and the JALR agu_sum check, but
its result feeds only a flop: ovr_q (reset 0) and ovr_tgt_q[31:2]
(is_jalr ? agu_sum[31:2] : alt_target[31:2], computed without the decision).
Set ovr_q when redirect_raw && !stall_ex_mem && !ovr_q. Hold it while
ovr_q && !fetch_ok, so the override stays pending until a word at the target
is actually fetched.
(2) F uses fetch_pc = ovr_q ? ovr_tgt_q : pc_q for io_imemAddr, the BHT read
index, the L0 index/tag (read and fill) and the predictor carry-select /
pc_inc. Use syn_preserve duplicates of ovr_q and of ovr_tgt_q[8:2] (like the
existing idx_* copies) so the select fanout is split. pc_q then loads the
usual pt ? ptgt : fetch_pc+4 on fetch_ok && accept. The redirect mux level on
pc_d disappears, and pc_en becomes fetch_ok && (accept || ovr_q).
(3) In an ovr_q cycle, redirect consumers are driven from the flop: IF/ID
accepts unconditionally and captures the target word (valid = fetch_ok), the
control-only ID/EX flush kills the wrong-path instruction in ID, and an EX
kill makes EX/MEM capture the wrong-path instruction in EX as a control-cleared
bubble (valid, reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, is_branch, is_jump, is_illegal
= 0). That EX instruction's own redirect and BHT training are suppressed, and
div_unit start is gated with !ovr_q. The branch sits in EX/MEM during the ovr_q
cycle and is never a mem op, so no dmem stall can coincide with the kill.
Timeline: branch in EX at t, target fetched at t+1, in ID at t+2 and in EX at
t+3, the same as today, so cycles stay ~3.55M. The worst path shrinks to
forward -> compare -> AND-OR -> one flop (about 7 levels). The next cones are
forward -> ALU/DSP -> alu_result (~10-10.5 ns on r4s2/r5s0) and the F cones,
which gain one flop-selected LUT level. Expected Fmax is ~95-100 MHz
(+8-14%), for a fitness gain of about +9%. Fallback if `make timing` shows the
F-head mux on the worst path: drop the override bypass and let pc_q load
ovr_tgt_q in the ovr_q cycle (+1 cycle per redirect, ~+2.8% cycles).

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20260930-002-r7s1 (improvement, +5.20%): Registering the EX redirect into ovr_q/ovr_tgt_q and letting F fetch next cycle from a flop-selected fetch_pc = ovr_q ? ovr_tgt_q : pc_q kept the mispredict penalty unchanged (the target is still fetched at t+1) and scored 259.16 against 246.35, about 92.1 MHz if cycles stayed at 3,552,529 (inferred; no post-change timing report or cycle count was recorded), which is roughly 60% of the +9% (95-100 MHz) estimate; it worked because the redirect was the only EX signal that fanned into pc_en, pc_d, IF/ID valid and the ID/EX flush (r6s1's 24-cell worst path), and dropping the redirect mux from pc_d probably also shortened r6s1's IF cones that end at pc_q (imem->carry-select->pc_d and L0 index->LUTRAM->pt->pc_d); the likely cap is that the r6s1 report had five cones within 0.03 ns, and the untouched ALU cone (opa_val->forward->adder->case mux) and the rs1->load-use->ID/EX sync-reset cone probably set the new period, while the implementer also indexed the L0 by pc_q and disabled its lookup in override cycles, so a redirect target that would have hit in L0 now waits for imem_ready (a small, unmeasured cycle cost); its five syn_preserve copies of ovr_q did not stall formal, which fits r7s0's inference that only copies of RVFI-observed nets such as the regfile address hurt; so when a late control signal fans into several stages, register it and bypass the fetch address from the flop, then run `make timing` and cosim before aiming the next cut at the ALU and load-use cones (r7s0's groups without its regfile-address copies).

title: Predictor pass on the L0 champion: late-resolve load->branch (no load-use bubble for predicted branches) folded into existing muxes, plus an 8-entry F-stage return-address stack
motivation:
The champion (r6s1: 246.35, 87.5 MHz, 3,552,529 cycles for 2,922,015
retired instructions) hides most istall cycles behind its L0 loop
cache. Of the ~630k non-retiring cycles that remain, the predictor
side owns two measured chunks:
  - Load-use bubbles in front of a BRANCH that consumes a LOAD. Of the
    203,959 adjacent LOAD->consumer pairs, 135,320 have a conditional
    branch as the consumer (r6s2 trace study). r5s2 removed that
    bubble for predicted aligned branches by resolving them one stage
    late in MEM, flop to flop against MEM/WB.wb_data. It measured
    4,056,705 vs 4,188,685 cycles (-132k, -3.15%) with Fmax held at
    97.07 MHz. On today's 3.55M-cycle base the same ~-120k to -130k
    is -3.4% to -3.7%.
  - Returns. All 13,735 JALRs in the timed window are returns and an
    8-entry RAS hits 13,734 of them. Since r6s1 added the registered
    IF/ID, every EX redirect costs 2 bubbles, so returns cost ~27.5k
    cycles (0.77%).
The direction BHT itself is nearly saturated (39.8k mispredicts at 512
entries; gshare/tournament up to 2K entries only reach 32.6k-36k, a
~0.4% gain), so it is left alone.
r6s0 stacked the same late resolve and lost Fmax. The cause was not the
compare but a new `else if (late_redirect) pc_q <= late_target`
priority level placed after the critical redirect/agu_sum cone. The
champion's worst path is exactly that cone: EX/MEM.alu_result ->
forward -> compare -> redirect -> ID/EX flush (u_id/valid_q), 16.73 ns
arrival. So any late-redirect term must enter only as an early flop
side input folded into LUTs that already exist.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two predictor-side IPC changes, neither adding a LUT level to the EX
redirect cone or to the L0 hit -> pc_en cone. Implement A first and
run cosim, then add B.

A. Late-resolve load->branch (port of r5s2, rewired to the L0 core).
 1. Hazard. When the IF/ID word is an aligned-target BRANCH, predecode
    it in F from the word already muxed into IF/ID (opcode 1100011,
    funct3 not 2/3, instr[8]==0) and store it as a registered
    if_id.late_ok bit. If load_use_hazard fires only because of this
    branch, do not stall. The branch enters ID/EX with late=1. Its
    one-hot sel_* go into separate late_sel_* flops, and its EX sel_*
    are zero, so EX's redirect equation is unchanged. late1/late2 are
    the registered fwd1_ex/fwd2_ex matches. JALR, misaligned-target
    branches and every non-branch consumer keep the load-use stall.
    Compute this as load_use_raw && !(if_id.late_ok) from flops only,
    so backend_stall gets no deeper.
 2. EX. A late branch does no EX redirect and no EX BHT training. It
    passes late_sel_*, late1/late2, alt_target, pred, bht_ctr and the
    post-forward rs1/rs2 (EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val already exist for
    RVFI) into EX/MEM.
 3. MEM. The load is in MEM/WB now. Build
    op1 = late1 ? MEM/WB.wb_data : EX/MEM.rs1_val, and op2 the same way
    (flop selects). Take eq and one 33-bit borrow compare for lt/ltu,
    AND-OR them with late_sel_*, and register the result into
    late_redirect_q. Register late_target_q = alt_target. The whole
    cone is flop to flop and ends at 1-2 flops. The same cycle,
    register the late BHT training. The training write port becomes
    late_q ? late training : EX training (flop-selected, both from
    flops). A colliding EX training write is dropped; that only costs
    performance.
 4. Late redirect (the cycle after MEM). Fold it in; do not add a
    priority branch:
    - EX: redirect_all = redirect | late_redirect_q. OR the flop into
      the last LUT of the existing redirect AND-OR, or into the
      pc_en / IF/ID-kill / ID/EX-flush consumers as a spare LUT input,
      whichever keeps the level count. redirect_target becomes
      late_redirect_q ? late_target_q : (is_jalr ? agu : alt_target).
      Put the flop select on the early alt_target_q side, so it stays
      a 3:1 with two flop-driven selects and agu_sum as the only late
      input.
    - While late_redirect_q is high, the EX-stage instruction is
      wrong-path. Kill its EX/MEM capture (valid, reg_write,
      mem_read, mem_write, is_illegal, is_branch, late), its EX
      redirect (gate the sel_*/is_jalr terms with !late_redirect_q
      through spare flop inputs of the first-level LUTs) and its BHT
      write, and block or abort a div_unit start (abort input). IF/ID
      and ID/EX are cleared by the normal redirect path. No wrong-path
      instruction has written memory or the regfile: a store writes
      only in MEM, and it is killed at EX/MEM capture.
 5. RVFI. In MEM, correct rs?_val with the MEM/WB value when late1/2,
    and recompute pc_next (branch_target vs pc+4) from the late
    outcome. This logic is RVFI-only and is pruned from the timed
    netlist.

B. 8-entry return-address stack in F.
 - Predecode, imem side: push = JAL or JALR with rd in {x1,x5}
   (pc+4). pop = the exact word `ret` (0x00008067, i.e. JALR x0, 0(x1)).
   It is a 32-bit constant compare that runs in parallel with the
   carry-select adder. On the L0 side, add one stored ret bit and one
   push bit to the L0 entry (filled from the same predecode), so a hit
   needs no compare.
 - pt gains `ret_ok && ras_nonempty`. ptgt gains TOS as one more source
   merged into the existing imem_ready select:
     ptgt = sel_tos ? tos : (imem_ready ? tgt_imem : l0_tgt)
   where sel_tos = imem_ready ? ret_imem : ret_l0. That is one LUT5/6
   per bit, with TOS and sel_tos arriving before the adder output. The
   redirect mux stays last on pc_d.
 - The stack is 8 x 30-bit flops with a 3-bit TOS pointer. It is
   updated only when F hands a word to IF/ID (fetch_ok && accept &&
   !redirect). The pointer is carried in if_id_t/id_ex_t. On any EX
   (or late) redirect the pointer is restored from the redirecting
   instruction's copy (pointer repair only, no content repair; an
   overwritten entry costs one mispredict, never correctness).
 - A predicted return carries pred_ret=1 into ID/EX, with its
   predicted target in a new ret_tgt field (TOS). Its alt_target is
   pc+4, the architectural next PC if the return traps.
 - Verification stays off the EX redirect cone. The existing EX JALR
   redirect term becomes is_jalr && !pred_ret && !agu_sum[1], where
   pred_ret is a spare flop input. For a predicted return
   (imm = 0, so the target is rs1), EX computes
   ret_mis = (rs1[31:2] != ret_tgt[31:2]) || rs1[1] from the
   post-forward rs1. That cone has the same depth as cmp_eq. The
   result is only registered into part A's late_redirect_q, with
   late_target_q = rs1[1] ? alt_target : {rs1[31:2],2'b00}. If part A's
   MEM late redirect fires in the same cycle, it is older and wins.
   A mispredicted return costs 3 cycles, but mispredicts are
   ~1 in 13.7k returns. Every correct return now costs 0 cycles
   instead of 2.
 - Late-redirect kill rule, shared by A and B. On the cycle
   late_redirect_q is high, the instruction in EX is wrong-path, and
   its EX/MEM capture, redirect, BHT write and div start are killed.
   For part A, the instruction one ahead of that (in EX while the
   late branch is in EX/MEM) is also wrong-path. Kill its EX/MEM
   capture with the combinational MEM-local late_mis: flop -> compare
   -> AND into the EX/MEM control D inputs, a short path. That way no
   wrong-path store ever reaches the dmem port, and a div it started
   is aborted.
 - Unpredicted JALRs (empty stack, non-ret JALR) redirect exactly as
   today.

Expected cycles: A saves ~-120k (r5s2 measured -132k; subtract ~+10k
for late mispredicts, which cost one more cycle than stall + EX
redirect). B saves ~-27k. Together: 3.55M -> ~3.40M (-4.2%). Fmax
target: unchanged at ~87.5 MHz, because every new term is either flop
to flop (MEM compare) or an early flop side input into LUTs that
already exist. Run `make timing` after A and again after B; if B
costs more than ~1% Fmax, ship A alone.

title: L0 fanout/depth trim: registered fill port, per-consumer L0 RAMs with private read-index copies, and a 6-bit tag for a 32 KiB L0-eligible window
motivation:
The r7s1 champion (259.16 = 92.323 MHz x ~3.56M cycles) is now limited
by the L0 loop cache, not by EX. Its recorded worst path runs
cpu/u_if/idx_dat_q_0 -> cpu/u_if/idx_vld_q_6: only 7 cells / 5 logic
levels but ~10.8 ns, i.e. routing-dominated. That is the L0 data-RAM
index flop -> 128-deep async LUTRAM (8 banks of RAM16SDP4) -> 8:1 bank
mux -> pt / ptgt -> pc_d -> the PC and its index-copy flops. r7s2's
worst path also ended at idx_vld_q (via pc_d), so pc_d / pc_en of the
L0 PC is the cone to cut.
Why it is slow: l0_icache uses ONE index net for the read and the write
of each structure. dat_mem is 64 bits wide (instr + tgt[31:2] + 2
predecode bits), so every idx_dat_q bit drives both the RAD and WAD
pins of 128 RAM16SDP4 cells (~256 loads spread across the whole RAM
footprint), although only tgt/jal_ok/br_ok (32 bits) feed pc_d; the
32-bit instruction word only lands in the IF/ID payload. idx_vld_q
drives both the 128:1 valid read mux and the 128-way valid write
decoder; idx_tag_q drives both ports of the tag RAM. On the write side
the fill data come straight from imem_data and the carry-select
tgt_imem, so those already-critical imem -> predecode -> adder -> pc_d
nets also carry 8 bank DI loads per bit. The hit path adds an 11-bit
tag compare (pc[19:9]) = 3 LUT levels before fetch_ok -> pc_en, which
is the clock enable of pc_q + the index copies.
CoreMark's whole .text is 16,760 bytes (riscv size on
bench/programs/coremark.elf); link.ld puts code at 0x0, so every
timed-loop PC is below 32 KiB and pc[19:15] never varies.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the L0's size, policy, hit rate and the whole pipeline unchanged;
restructure only how its RAMs are addressed and fed, so the L0 -> pc_d
and L0 -> hit -> pc_en cones lose fanout and one LUT level.

A. Registered fill port (write one cycle late from staging flops).
   Every cycle capture fill_we_q <= we_ok && !flush, fill_idx_q <=
   pc_q[8:2], fill_tag_q, fill_instr_q <= imem_data, fill_tgt_q <=
   tgt_imem, fill_jal_q, fill_br_q. All RAM writes and the valid-bit set
   use fill_idx_q / fill_we_q. The read-index copies then drive only RAD
   pins and the valid read mux; imem_data / tgt_imem each gain one flop
   load instead of 8 bank DI pins. Correctness: an L0 entry is a pure
   function of its PC (instr, target, predecode are static for that PC),
   tag and data are written together from the same staging flops, and
   valid is only set by that write, so a hit always returns a matched
   {tag, word, target}; the one-cycle-late write can only turn a hit
   into a miss (same index re-fetched on the very next cycle while
   fetch_ok is high, i.e. only a jump-to-self), costing ~0 cycles.
   flush clears valid_q and squashes fill_we_q (flush still wins).
B. Split dat_mem by consumer: a next-PC RAM {tgt[31:2], jal_ok, br_ok}
   and an instruction RAM {instr}, each read through its own
   syn_preserve copy of pc_q[8:2] (idx_prd_q, idx_ins_q; same D and
   enable as pc_q, like the existing idx_tag/idx_dat/idx_vld). The
   pc_d cone then sees a 32-bit RAM whose index nets load 64 RAD pins
   instead of ~256 mixed pins; the instruction word's RAM can be placed
   near IF/ID without pulling the next-PC RAM away from pc_q.
C. Narrow the tag to pc[14:9] (6 bits, was 11) and make
   in_range = (pc_q[31:15] == 0) (was pc[31:20]); fill and hit both use
   it, so PCs >= 32 KiB just never use the L0 (still correct, only
   slower for code beyond 32 KiB; none in CoreMark). The 6-bit
   compare is 3 XNOR-pair LUT4s + one AND LUT with valid, one level
   shorter than 11 bits, and the tag RAM shrinks 11 -> 6 bits.
   in_range is a NOR of pc_q flops, computed in parallel with the RAM
   read.
The regfile address, RVFI-observed nets and everything past IF/ID stay
untouched (r7s0: copies of RVFI-observed nets stall formal; L0 index
copies did not).
Expected: cycles unchanged (~3.56M; the tag narrowing and late fill
cost ~0), the L0 cones shorten by ~0.8-1.2 ns (fanout-256 -> 64 index
nets, one fewer compare level, lighter tgt_imem/imem_data nets), and the
period drops until the next tier (EX forward -> ALU -> alu_result,
~10.26 ns on r4s2, and the BHT read -> pt -> pc_d cone) sets it:
~97-99 MHz, fitness ~272-278 (+5-7%). Implementer: run `make timing
TARGET=bench` before and after, and a quick cosim to confirm cycles.
If the BHT cone (fetch_pc mux -> 512-deep LUTRAM -> 32:1 -> pt ->
pc_d) becomes the worst path, give the BHT read its own syn_preserve
copies of ovr_tgt_q[10:2] / pc_q[10:2] and ovr_q so its address mux
does not share nets with the imem address and the carry-select adder.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r8s0 (regression, +1.71%): The L0 fanout trim (fill written one cycle late from staging flops, the 64-bit data RAM split into a next-PC RAM and an instruction RAM with their own syn_preserve read-index copies, and a 6-bit tag with the L0 limited to PCs below 32 KiB) took the L0 off the worst paths at no cycle cost (3,563,948 vs 3,562,334) and passed all 53 formal checks, but median Fmax rose only from 92.32 to 93.94 MHz (the implementer's all-options run), under the 4.6% bar, because the next tier was only ~0.19 ns behind: the EX forward (opa_val / MEM/WB wb_data) -> ALU -> alu_result cone and the EX redirect -> ovr_l0_q/ovr_pc_q cone, now tied within ~0.02 ns, and not the ~10.26 ns the hypothesis took from r4s2's stale report; so keep these L0 cuts, estimate an Fmax cut from the current core's report over all three place options (`make timing` runs only option 0, which read 76.49 MHz on the champion while the score takes the median, so use `python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options`), and cut the ALU-forward and redirect->ovr cones together in one iteration.

title: Split L0 into a narrow next-fetch-PC way (fill-time predicted npc, own index copy) and an off-loop instruction way, plus registered one-hot EX forward selects, cutting both tied cones of the champion
motivation:
`make timing TARGET=bench` on the r7s1 champion (place_option 0, 76.49 MHz)
shows two cones tied within 0.27 ns:
  A) 18.368 ns, 7 cells: u_if/idx_dat_q_0 -> u_l0 dat_mem LUTRAM -> 8:1 block
     mux -> pt (l0_jal_ok | l0_br_ok & bht_ctr[1]) -> pc_d (pt ? l0_tgt :
     pc_inc, then the imem_ready mux) -> pc_q / idx_*_q.  Only 5 logic levels:
     it is routing-bound, because the one idx_dat_q copy drives the address of
     all 128 RAM16SDP4 blocks of the 64-bit x 128 data array (16 wide x 8 deep)
     before the 8:1 output mux, and the BHT read (fetch_pc mux -> 32 RAM16 ->
     32:1 mux) also joins this cone through pt. The .tr report confirms it:
     idx_dat_q_0 has FANOUT 256 (read + write address of 128 blocks) and its
     net alone is 7.133 ns of the 13.04 ns data path; the RAM read, 3 mux
     levels, the pt?l0_tgt:pc_inc LUT and the imem_ready LUT are ~2.3 ns.
  B) 18.1-18.2 ns, 10 cells: u_id/data_q.fwd2_wb -> live-qualified 3:1 forward
     mux -> 32-bit eq/lt/ltu compare -> sel_* AND-OR -> redirect -> ovr_q /
     ovr_ex_q / ovr_id_q.
The median options (1, 2) are at 92.3 MHz with the same topology. Cutting
only one cone gains nothing (r5s0 lesson: the next tied cone sets the
period), so this hypothesis restructures the L0 so its data array is off the
PC loop, and applies the proven r4s0 registered-forward-select cut to cone B.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1) Two-way L0 (structural, cone A). Replace the single 64-bit-wide data
   array with two distributed-RAM arrays indexed by separate syn_preserve
   copies of pc_q[8:2]:
     - NPC way (19 bits/entry): npc[19:2] and pt, i.e. the *complete*
       predicted next fetch PC computed by the imem-side predictor at fill
       time (npc = pt_imem ? tgt_imem : pc_inc, already the imem arm of
       pc_d), so the BHT decision is frozen at fill. Fill is skipped when
       npc[31:20] != 0 (never happens inside the 1 MiB memory).
     - Instruction way (50 bits/entry): instr[31:0] and alt[19:2] (the
       alternative target IF/ID needs: pc+4 if pt, else the taken target).
   The read-index copies are further replicated per column group so no
   index flop drives more than ~16 RAM16 read addresses (e.g. 3 copies for the
   NPC way, 3 for the instruction way), and the fill (write) address comes
   from its own copies, halving the per-net load (the write port is
   flop-to-RAM and off every critical cone).
   On an L0 hit, pc_d = {12'b0, l0_npc} directly: the L0 side of the PC
   loop becomes idx_npc_q -> 40 RAM16 blocks (instead of 128) -> 8:1 mux ->
   final imem_ready mux -> D, with the pt LUT, the pt?tgt:pc_inc mux and the
   BHT read removed from it. The instruction way only feeds IF/ID data
   (a full cycle of slack). The BHT is still read every cycle for the imem
   arm and for the bht_ctr training snapshot, and every imem fetch refreshes
   the L0 entry (~78% of fetch cycles), so frozen predictions cost little
   accuracy; mispredictions are still caught in EX, so correctness is
   untouched. The tag/valid arrays keep their own index copies; l0_hit still
   gates pc_en exactly as now.
2) Registered one-hot forward selects (cone B, r4s0 cut, proven -0.8 ns on
   an older base). ID qualifies fwd?_ex / fwd?_wb with the reg_write values
   EX/MEM and MEM/WB are about to capture (ID/EX.reg_write && !misalign_jump
   via a 2-bit JALR carry of agu_sum[1], EX/MEM.reg_write && !mem_misalign),
   resolves EX/MEM-over-MEM/WB priority, and registers mutually exclusive
   sel_ex / sel_wb / sel_rf flops, so EX's rs1/rs2/alu_a/alu_b are one
   flop-driven AND-OR in front of the comparator/ALU and the fanout-130
   MEM/WB.reg_write net leaves the redirect cone. The regfile read address
   and x0 read arm stay on the RVFI-observed nets (r7s0 lesson).

fanout-~16-32 net, plus one LUT level), so it leaves the top tier, cone
B ~0.8 ns; the period then lands on the next tier (imem->carry-select->pc_d,
BHT->pt_imem->pc_d, ALU/DSP), estimated ~97-100 MHz (+5-8%). Cycles should be
within +/-0.5% (frozen L0 predictions vs 3,562,334).

title: Speculate predicted branches past load-use on the registered-redirect core: MEM late-verify as a second ovr_q source, load-use taken off the ID/EX datapath enable
motivation:
Direction-predictor headroom is gone: the 512x2b bimodal BHT mispredicts
39.8k of 529.6k branches and gshare/tournament up to 2K entries only
reach 32.6k-36k (~0.3% of cycles). The largest predictor-shaped loss left
is the load-use bubble in front of an already-predicted branch: 135,320
of the 203,959 adjacent LOAD->consumer pairs in the timed CoreMark window
have a conditional BRANCH as the consumer (list walks, `if (*p == x)`,
state-machine loops). IF has already predicted the branch and is fetching
the predicted path, so the bubble buys nothing unless the prediction is
wrong. r5s2 measured this exactly on r4s2 (4,188,685 -> 4,056,705 cycles,
-3.15%, Fmax held). Since r6s1's L0 cache hides most istalls, more of
these pairs now arrive back to back, so on the champion (~3.56M cycles,
92.3 MHz) the saving should be ~120-130k cycles (-3.4 to -3.7%). This is
confirmed by measurement: r7s2 built the same late resolve on the r6s1
L0 core and the log records 3,425,336 cycles vs 3,552,529 (-127k,
-3.6%). Only its Fmax (80.4 MHz) failed, and that came from the wiring
described below, not from the compare.
Two ports failed on Fmax, both for wiring reasons LESSONS.md pinned down:

Direction-predictor headroom is gone: the 512x2b bimodal BHT mispredicts
39.8k of 529.6k branches and gshare/tournament up to 2K entries only
reach 32.6k-36k (~0.3% of cycles). The largest predictor-shaped loss left
is the load-use bubble in front of an already-predicted branch: 135,320
of the 203,959 adjacent LOAD->consumer pairs in the timed CoreMark window
have a conditional BRANCH as the consumer (list walks, `if (*p == x)`,
state-machine loops). IF has already predicted the branch and is fetching
the predicted path, so the bubble buys nothing unless the prediction is
wrong. r5s2 measured this exactly on r4s2 (4,188,685 -> 4,056,705 cycles,
-3.15%, Fmax held). Since r6s1's L0 cache hides most istalls, more of
these pairs now arrive back to back, so on the champion (~3.56M cycles,

confirmed by measurement: r7s2 built the same late resolve on the r6s1
L0 core and the log records 3,425,336 cycles vs 3,552,529 (-127k,
-3.6%). Only its Fmax (80.4 MHz) failed, and that came from the wiring
described below, not from the compare.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three parts, built in this order, with `make timing` after part 1.

1. (Fmax, prerequisite) Take load-use off the ID/EX datapath enable.
   On a load-use bubble the IF/ID entry is held and re-decoded next cycle,
   so ID/EX's datapath payload (data_q: pc, rs?_val, opa/opb_val, imm,
   fwd bits, instr, alt_target, ...) is don't-care for the bubble and may
   capture freely. Change id_stage so data_q's enable is
   !(dmem_stall || div_stall) only (export a separate `hold_id` from
   hazard_unit), while the ~17 control flops keep reset||flush with flush
   = (load_use || ovr) && !dmem_stall and stall as today. Also register a
   single ID/EX flop `ld_nz_q = v && dec_mem_read && instr[11:7] != 0` so
   hazard_unit's load_use is one LUT4 of flops+compares:
   ld_nz_q & !late_ok & (rd==rs1 | rd==rs2).

2. (Predictor) Late resolve of a predicted, aligned conditional branch
   that consumes the LOAD in ID/EX.
   - IF: add one IF/ID bit late_ok_q = aligned BRANCH predecode
     (imem_ready ? br_ok : l0_br_ok, both already exist; flop-selected).
   - hazard_unit: load_use no longer fires when late_ok_q (see part 1),
     so the branch enters ID/EX right behind the load.
   - id_stage: compute late1/late2 = late_ok && id_ex.mem_read && rs? ==
     id_ex.rd (non-x0). For such a branch clear the EX sel_* selects (EX
     never redirects on it; its EX compare sees the load's address) and
     register one-hot late_sel_* (same prediction folding as sel_*) plus
     late1_q/late2_q. These only land on ID/EX flop D inputs.
   - ex_stage: carry late_sel_*, late1/2, pred, bht_ctr and the
     alternative target (the existing alt_target_q, i.e. pc+4 if
     predicted taken else pc+imm) into EX/MEM. The EX/MEM rs?_val for a
     late operand is don't-care (overwritten in MEM).
   - mem_stage: flop-to-flop compare in MEM:
       a = late1_q ? MEM/WB.wb_data : EX/MEM.rs1_val
       b = late2_q ? MEM/WB.wb_data : EX/MEM.rs2_val
       late_mis = OR(late_sel_* & {eq,!eq,lt,!lt,ltu,!ltu}(a,b))
     (one 33-bit subtract/borrow + eq, ~5 levels, starts at flops).
     If the load in MEM/WB trapped (MEM/WB.ctrl.is_illegal / reg_write
     cleared), treat it as a replay instead: kill the branch at MEM/WB
     capture and redirect to the branch's own PC, so a trapping load can
     never feed a stale operand (rare; keeps formal exact).
   - Redirect: late_mis becomes a second source of the existing fetch
     override. In if_stage: ovr_d = redirect || late_mis || (ovr_q &&
     !imem_ready) (one more input on the 5 ovr flops, whose cone ends
     there), and ovr_tgt_q loads late_mis ? EX/MEM.late_alt : redirect_
     target (priority to the older, late instruction; it is a flop-side
     select on the ovr_tgt_q D input, not on pc_d/pc_en). pc_q, pc_d,
     pc_en and the L0 index copies are untouched.
   - Kill: on late_mis the instruction in EX at the same cycle is wrong
     path: add late_mis to ex_stage's kill for the EX/MEM capture (same
     control-only clear as ovr_ex, so a wrong-path store never reaches
     MEM), to div_valid (no divide start) and to bht_we. The next cycle is
     an ordinary ovr_q cycle (ID flushed, EX killed, IF/ID refilled from
     the target), so a late mispredict costs 3 cycles = today's bubble +
     2-cycle EX mispredict, i.e. never worse than today.
   - BHT training for a late branch comes from MEM (actual = pred ^
     late_mis) through the existing registered write port; on a same-cycle
     collision with an EX branch keep either one (performance only).
   - RVFI (pruned by synthesis): MEM/WB.rs?_val use a/b above and
     MEM/WB.pc_next is recomputed as pred^late_mis ? target : pc+4.

3. Keep everything else of r7s1 as is (ovr copies, L0 indexed by pc_q,
   carry-select target, mispredict-only EX redirect).

Expected: cycles 3.56M -> ~3.44M (-3.5%) from part 2, and part 1 removes
the load-use compare from the enable of ~400 ID/EX datapath flops (r6s1's
C3 cone, one of the ~0.03 ns tied cones), so Fmax should hold or rise
1-3% from 92.3 MHz. Target fitness ~268-275 (+4 to +6%).
Validation: run formal insn_beq_ch0/insn_bne_ch0/insn_lw_ch0 + reg_ch0
and pc_fwd early (the late path changes rs1/rs2_rdata sourcing), cosim
`--bench --istall --dstall` for the cycle count, and `make timing` after
part 1 and after part 2.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r8s2 (regression, -8.94%): Re-stacking the late load->branch resolve on r7s1's registered-redirect core, wired as LESSONS advised (load-use taken off the ID/EX datapath enable, the late mispredict made a second source of ovr_q/ovr_tgt_q), scored 235.99, which puts Fmax at about 81 MHz if cycles fell by the ~127k r7s2 measured (84 MHz even if they did not) against 92.3, so it landed where r7s2 did (80.36 MHz) despite different redirect wiring; the only Fmax-neutral version, r5s2, registered the MEM compare into late_redirect_q before any use, but here the so-called flop-to-flop compare (MEM/WB.wb_data -> 33-bit borrow/eq -> late_sel_* AND-OR) fed same-cycle consumers combinationally: the ovr_q copies and the select of the 30-bit ovr_tgt_q mux, a new `late_kill` on the EX/MEM control clear (in r7s1 the only EX kill is the ovr_ex flop), the BHT write-port select and `div_unit.start`; that gives a cone about as deep as the EX redirect with more fanout, and it also loads every wb_data bit that already sits on the tied wb_data -> forward -> ALU cone (inferred: no timing report or cycle count was recorded, so which of these sets the period is unknown); so count a compare as flop-to-flop only if its result lands in one register, bring the late resolve back only in r5s2's form (late_redirect_q ORed into ovr_d as a flop, with the two younger instructions killed at the next capture, costing one extra cycle per late mispredict), and bundle it with an orthogonal Fmax gain, because its ~3.6% cycle cut cannot clear the 4.6% bar alone.

title: Rebuild r8s0's L0 trim, then register the forward selects and use a forward-only copy of MEM/WB wb_data
motivation:
The score is the 3-option median, and options 1 and 2 have always matched
each other. Measured data from the log:
  - r7s1 champion: [76.49, 92.32, 92.32] MHz, 3,562,334 cycles. Option 0's
    worst path is the L0 index idx_dat_q -> idx_vld_q (7 cells, routing-bound:
    idx_dat_q has fanout 256).
  - r8s0 (the L0 trim alone): [88.30, 93.94, 93.94] MHz, 3,563,948 cycles,
    formal passed. The worst path moved to
    u_mem/reg_q.ctrl.reg_write -> live-qualified EX forward mux -> ALU ->
    u_ex/reg_q.alu_result_7 (7 cells). The redirect -> ovr_q cone is tied
    with it within ~0.02 ns, and it starts on the same forward mux
    (fwd?_wb/MEM/WB.reg_write -> forward -> eq/lt/ltu -> sel AND-OR -> ovr_d).
  - r4s0 registered priority-resolved forward selects on an older base and
    saved ~0.8 ns. Its worst path, and r5s0's (101.3 MHz), then became
    u_mem/reg_q.wb_data_1 -> forward -> ALU -> alu_result (6 cells).
So once the L0 is trimmed, the next two tiers are known and share one
entry point: two flops at the MEM/WB boundary, each with a large fanout.
- MEM/WB.ctrl.reg_write drives the regfile write enable decode, both
  write-first bypass compares and all 4x32 EX forward-mux bits.
- MEM/WB.wb_data drives each bit into 31 regfile D pins, the two ID bypass
  muxes and the 4 EX forward muxes, about 37 loads spread across the
  ~1000-flop regfile footprint.
Neither net has to be on the EX cone. r8s1 tried registered selects, but it
lost because of its L0 rewrite: the fill index went through the override
mux and its unstaged NPC way fell to 86.97 MHz on options 1/2. The selects
were not the cause.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Four cuts in priority order. A and B are mandatory, C is a few lines, and D
is optional if time allows. The pipeline, predictor, L0 policy, fetch
override and cycle count all stay the same.

A. Rebuild r8s0's L0 trim exactly as specified (its RTL is not in git).
   Measured +1.7% with no cycle cost.
   - Registered fill port: stage fill_we_q (= we_ok && !flush), fill_idx_q
     (= pc_q[8:2]), fill tag, instr, tgt_imem, jal_ok and br_ok in flops.
     Write the tag RAM, both data RAMs and the valid bit from those flops
     one cycle later. flush clears valid_q and squashes fill_we_q.
   - Split dat_mem into a next-PC RAM {tgt, jal_ok, br_ok} and an
     instruction RAM, each read through its own syn_preserve copy of
     pc_q[8:2] (idx_prd_q, idx_ins_q), with the same D and enable as pc_q.
   - Tag = pc[14:9] (6 bits) and in_range = pc_q[31:15] == 0. CoreMark's
     .text is 16.7 KiB at 0x0.
   - Do NOT route any fill index through the override mux, and do NOT write
     any RAM from an unstaged critical cone. Those were r8s1's mistakes.

B. Registered one-hot forward selects (the r4s0 cut). ID already knows the
   reg_write values that EX/MEM and MEM/WB will capture on the same edge
   that ID/EX captures a real instruction. Every stall that blocks them
   also holds or bubbles ID/EX, div_stall holds ID/EX, and a kill coincides
   with flush_id.
   - ex_rw_next = ID/EX.ctrl.reg_write && !misalign_jump.
     - For JAL, misalign_jump = imm[1] (a flop).
     - For JALR it is agu1 = rs1[1] ^ imm[1] ^ (rs1[0] & imm[0]): one LUT on
       the forwarded rs1[1:0]. Export it from ex_stage.
   - wb_rw_next = EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write && !mem_misalign, exported from
     mem_stage (flop-only inputs).
   - ID computes, for rs1 and rs2:
     s_ex = match_ex && ex_rw_next
     s_wb = match_wb && wb_rw_next && !s_ex
     s_rf = !(s_ex | s_wb)
   - It also computes the ALU-operand versions (sa_* masked by use_pc,
     sb_* masked by use_imm, whose _rf arm selects opa_val / opb_val).
   - All 12 bits are registered into ID/EX in place of fwd1/2_ex/wb and
     fwda/b_ex/wb.
   EX's four operand muxes become flop-driven AND-ORs:
     ({32{s_ex}} & EX/MEM.alu_result) | ({32{s_wb}} & fwd_wb) | ({32{s_rf}} & val)
   This takes MEM/WB.reg_write and EX/MEM.reg_write out of the ALU and
   redirect cones entirely. Leave rs1_addr/rs2_addr, the regfile read
   address and its x0 arm on the RVFI-observed nets (r7s0 lesson).

C. Forward-only copy of MEM/WB wb_data. In mem_stage, add
   `(* syn_preserve = 1 *) logic [31:0] fwd_wb_q` with exactly the
   reg_q.wb_data D, reset and enable (reset -> 0; hold_wb -> hold; else
   wb_data), and export it as the EX forward source.
   - The regfile write, the ID write-first bypass and RVFI keep
     reg_q.wb_data.
   - The copy's fanout is 4 per bit instead of ~37, so it can sit next to
     the EX forward/ALU LUTs. That is the head of r4s0's and r5s0's
     post-cut worst path (wb_data_1 -> alu_result).
   - It is a same-D copy like the five ovr_q copies, which passed formal. It
     is not a different-D copy like r7s0's regfile-address copies.

D. (If time allows) Single borrow compare on the redirect cone.
   - ID merges sel_ltu into sel_lt and sel_geu into sel_ge, and registers
     cmp_signed = !funct3[1].
   - EX computes lt from one 33-bit compare,
     $signed({s & rs1[31], rs1}) < $signed({s & rs2[31], rs2}), and
     redirect_raw = sel_eq&eq | sel_ne&!eq | sel_lt&lt | sel_ge&!lt |
     is_jalr&!agu1, which saves 2 terms and one comparator ahead of ovr_d.
   - BHT training keeps using redirect_raw.

Expected result:
- A alone was 93.94 MHz.
- B removes the reg_write level and its fanout from both tied cones. On the
  r3s0 base this saved ~0.8 ns.
- C lightens the next tier's start net.
- The next tier is expected to be the ALU cone at about 100 MHz (r5s0
  reached 101.3 with the same wb_data start).
- Target: ~98-100 MHz at ~3.564M cycles, i.e. fitness ~275-280 (+6-8%).

Implementer:
- Check with `python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options`, not
  option 0 alone.
- Run cosim to confirm cycles stay near 3.564M.
- Run insn_add_ch0, insn_jalr_ch0 and reg_ch0 before submitting.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r9s0 (improvement, +4.72%): Rebuilding r8s0's L0 trim and stacking two cuts on it cleared the 4.6% bar that the trim alone missed (93.94 MHz, +1.71%): r4s0's registered one-hot forward selects, qualified in ID with ex_rw_next/wb_rw_next exported from EX and MEM, and a syn_preserve forward-only copy of MEM/WB wb_data, which feeds only the 4 EX forward muxes instead of ~37 loads per bit while the regfile, ID bypass and RVFI keep reg_q.wb_data; it scored 271.38 against 259.16, about 96.7 MHz if cycles stayed near r8s0's 3,563,948 (inferred; no per-option timing or cycle count was recorded), and since it was scored, the same-D copy passed formal like the ovr_q copies and unlike r7s0's different-D regfile-address copies; but the two cuts saved only ~0.3 ns on top of the trim, against the ~0.8 ns r4s0 measured on an older base and the 98-100 MHz target, and optional part D (one borrow compare in place of the separate lt/ltu compares) was not built, so the limiting cone is unknown: either the redirect -> ovr_q cone, which still has its three comparators after the flop-selected forward, or the next ALU/IF tier; so keep a sub-bar Fmax cut and re-stack it once its tied partner is cut in the same iteration, expect a cut on a ~10 ns core to save well under what it saved on an older base, and build D next, checking the median with `python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options`.

title: Per-source IF next-PC datapaths (pc_q and ovr_tgt_q successors computed in parallel, selected late) plus r8s0's L0 trim, registered one-hot EX forward selects and flop-sourced BHT training, cutting all four tied cones of the champion
motivation:
`python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options --paths 12` on the champion
(this worktree, r7s1 RTL) gives 92.323 MHz on the two median options (1, 2;
option 0 is the 76.49 L0 outlier). Their top 12 paths are three distinct
cones tied within 0.07 ns (16.126 .. 16.059 ns arrival):
  A) IF, 27-28 cells: cpu/u_if/ovr_pc_q -> fetch_pc mux (30 bits) ->
     pc_inc incrementer / carry-select pc+imm adder -> pt ? ptgt : pc_inc ->
     pc_q[31:28] and data_q.alt_target[31:28]; plus 11 cells ovr_pc_q ->
     fetch_pc[10:2] -> BHT LUTRAM read -> pt -> pc_d[8:2] -> idx_tag_q. This
     cone was created by r7s1: the fetch-override mux sits IN FRONT of both
     adders and the BHT index, so the high-fanout ovr_pc_q flop starts the
     carry chains.
  B) EX, 6 cells: cpu/u_mem/reg_q.ctrl.reg_write (live MEM/WB qualifier,
     fanout ~130) -> 3:1 forward mux -> ALU -> alu_result; and 38 cells
     u_id/data_q.fwda_wb -> forward -> adder -> alu_result[30].
  C) EX, 11 cells: u_id/data_q.fwd2_wb -> forward mux -> 32-bit compare ->
     redirect_raw -> br_taken_act -> ctr_new -> bht_wdata (the same compare
     also feeds redirect -> ovr_q copies).
  D) IF, 10.672 ns data delay (0.12 ns behind): u_if/idx_tag_q_3 -> L0 tag
     LUTRAM -> 11-bit tag compare + pc[31:20] range -> hit -> fetch_ok ->
     pc_en = CE of pc_q and the idx_*_q copies. r8s0's L0 trim (registered
     fill, split next-PC / instruction RAMs with private read-index copies,
     6-bit tag, L0 limited to PCs < 32 KiB; CoreMark .text is 16.7 KB) took
     this cone off the worst paths at no cycle cost (median 92.32 -> 93.94).
LESSONS r5s0/r8s0/r8s1: cutting one tied cone gains nothing, so all four
must go in one iteration, and every cut must be judged on the 3-option median.

D (first, port verbatim): r8s0's L0 trim as recorded in log.jsonl
(hyp-20261001-001-r8s0): staged fill port, npc/instruction RAM split with

of muxing the source in front of it. Compute from flops, in parallel:
inc_p = pc_q + 1, inc_o = ovr_tgt_q + 1, and the carry-select predicted
target for both bases (lo_sum_p/lo_sum_o = base[20:2] + imm_lo, hi taken
as base[31:21] / +1 / -1, all precomputed from the respective flop).
Duplicate the 512x2 BHT (both copies written by the same training port; one
read with pc_q[10:2], one with ovr_tgt_q[10:2], ~32 extra RAM16 cells).
Only after the adders / RAM reads select by a syn_preserve copy of the
override flop: tgt_imem, pc_inc and bht_ctr = ovr ? *_o : *_p. In an
override cycle fetch_ok = imem_ready, so the L0 side is untouched. The
ovr_pc_q -> carry-chain start and the 30-bit fetch_pc fanout disappear from
the PC loop; imem_addr and IF/ID.pc keep a plain fetch_pc mux (flop to
flop / LED-only). Split the remaining select fanout over 2-3 syn_preserve
copies (target mux, inc mux, bht mux).
B (EX forward): ID computes priority-resolved, reg_write-qualified one-hot
selects for rs1, rs2, alu_a, alu_b using the values EX/MEM and MEM/WB are
about to capture (ID/EX.reg_write && !misalign_jump, where JALR needs only
the 2-bit agu_sum[1] carry; EX/MEM.reg_write && !mem_misalign), registers
them in ID/EX and zeroes the rs?_val / opa/opb payload when a forward is
selected, so each EX operand is (sel_ex & EX/MEM.alu_result) |
(sel_wb & MEM/WB.wb_data) | payload_q with no live reg_write term (r4s0
measured ~0.8 ns for this). Keep rs1_addr/rs2_addr and the regfile x0 arm
on the RVFI-observed nets (r7s0 formal lesson).

title: Registered MEM-stage resolve for load-fed branches (r5s2 form) + r8s0 L0 trim
motivation:
Direction-predictor headroom is gone: the 512x2b bimodal BHT mispredicts
39.8k of 529.6k branches and all 13.7k JALRs are returns, so at the
current 2-cycle redirect penalty every remaining mispredict + return
costs only ~107k cycles (3.0% of 3,562,334), and gshare/RAS can recover
at most a fraction of that while adding logic to the IF pc_d cone and the
EX redirect cone. The biggest branch-related loss left is the load-use
bubble in front of a branch that consumes the LOAD: ~105k cycles (~3%)
per r5s2's trace study. r5s2 (on r4s2) removed it Fmax-neutrally because
its MEM compare landed in ONE flop (late_redirect_q) before any use; the
two re-stacks that fed the compare combinationally into ovr_q copies,
the ovr_tgt mux select, EX/MEM kill, BHT port and div start (r7s2 at
80.4 MHz, r8s2 at 81.0 MHz) lost ~12% Fmax. LESSONS says: bring it back
only in r5s2's registered form, and bundle it with an orthogonal Fmax
gain because ~2.7% cycles cannot clear the 4.6% bar alone. r8s0's L0
fanout trim is exactly that: proven +1.7% median Fmax (92.32 -> 93.94)
at zero cycle cost, 53/53 formal passes.
